A **cadence** is how a phrase ends. Every ending has a different feel, and the feel comes from the
two chords that make it. This lesson plays the five you will meet most, each as a four-bar phrase, and
then asks a harder question about one of them: is it a cadence at all?

**How to use the page.** Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

## 1. The authentic cadence: V7 to I

**C, F, G7, C.** The strongest ending there is. G7 contains the leading tone B and the note F, which
are a tritone apart. Both are unstable: B wants to rise a half step to C and F wants to fall a half
step to E. The tonic chord that follows is where they land. The bass falls a fifth, and everything
leans the same way.

<div class="bl-step" data-step="auth"></div>

Learn this one first. Every other ending on the page is compared with it.

## 2. The half cadence: ending on V

**C, F, C, G.** The phrase stops on the dominant, with the tension still in the air. It is a comma,
not a full stop: the ear expects an answer, and the next phrase usually supplies it.

<div class="bl-step" data-step="half"></div>

## 3. The deceptive cadence: V7 to vi

**C, F, G7, Am.** Everything points at C, and then the last chord is Am, which shares two notes
with C (C and E). The leading tone still rises to C, but the chord on top of it is Am.
The listener expects a full stop and gets a surprise.

<div class="bl-step" data-step="decep"></div>

## 4. The plagal cadence, and why it is the fake one

**C, Am, F, C.** IV to I, the "Amen". Most books call this a cadence. This lesson does not, and
here is the argument.

- **A cadence is made by the dominant.** What ends a phrase in tonal music is the leading tone rising
  to the tonic and the tritone of V7 resolving inward. IV to I has neither. No note in F is pulled
  toward C, so nothing is resolved.
- **IV is a neighbour of I.** I, IV, I leaves home and comes back, exactly as I, vi, I does. That
  is a prolongation of the tonic chord, not an arrival.
- **It comes after the real cadence.** The "Amen" at the end of a hymn follows a V to I that has
  already closed the phrase. The plagal is tacked on afterwards, so it cannot be what made the ending.
- **Some theorists agree.** William Caplin's *Classical Form* counts only authentic and half
  cadences, and does not count IV to I as a cadence.

<div class="bl-step" data-step="plagal"></div>

Here is the "Amen" in its usual place: an authentic cadence first, then the plagal after it. Listen
to bars 1 and 2, which end the phrase, and then to bars 3 and 4, which only soften it.

<div class="bl-step" data-step="amen"></div>

There is a fair reply. In the blues, in gospel and in much rock, IV to I really is how a tune ends,
because those styles never relied on a leading tone. So whether "fake" means "not a cadence" or "a
different kind of ending" depends on the style. In the classical tradition the first reading is the
one with the support.

## 5. The backdoor: ♭VII to I

**C, F, B♭, C.** The chord on the flat seventh is B♭, and it falls a whole step to C. There is no
leading tone here either. The ending sounds relaxed, a door left open instead of shut. Compare it
with the plagal ending: both arrive without a dominant.

<div class="bl-step" data-step="flat7"></div>

## Test your ear

Two questions. The first asks which ending the band played. The second plays one of three endings and asks how the last chord feels, so you can decide for yourself whether the plagal is a cadence.

## Where to go next

- Play the five endings in a row at the same tempo and note which ones you could end a song on.
- Take any of the phrases to **Tools → Backing Track** (*Copy as ABC*, then paste into *Edit the changes (ABC)*) to choose the bass line and drums.
- The lesson on [borrowed chords](borrowed-chords.qmd) starts from the ♭VII to I ending.
